common_name: Lemon Drops African Iris (Compact Hybrid Fortnight Lily)

planting.note: Set out container-grown divisions in spring or fall into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this hybrid selection stays noticeably tighter and more compact than either straight-species parent, so space it closer than typical African iris plantings.

directions: Lemon Drops is a compact hybrid combining traits of Dietes iridioides and Dietes bicolor, producing darker, finer-textured evergreen foliage than either parent along with creamy-white, iris-like flowers marked with warm brown blotches at the base of each petal. Like other fortnight lilies, individual blooms last only a day but appear in rapid, repeating flushes from the same branching stalks through the warm months, so spent stems should be left in place rather than cut back. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates part shade with a slight reduction in flowering. Once established it needs little supplemental water and is well suited to smaller beds, containers, and foundation plantings where the larger species types would be oversized.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Orange Drops African Iris (Compact Hybrid Fortnight Lily)

planting.note: Set out container-grown divisions in spring or fall into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Orange Drops forms a dense, low clump and reblooms in flushes rather than a single flush, so plant where its off-and-on color through the growing season can be appreciated up close.

directions: Orange Drops is a dense-clumping Dietes hybrid selected for its ivory flowers marked with warm yellow-orange blotches, a deeper color accent than the plain white or pale-yellow tones typical of the wild African iris species. It shares the family habit of reblooming from the same wiry, branching flower stems over many weeks, so avoid cutting stalks back until they stop setting new buds. Plant in full sun for maximum flower production, though it also performs acceptably in bright part shade. Deer generally avoid it, and once roots are established it needs only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells, making it a tidy, low-input choice for mixed borders, medians, and mass plantings.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after all danger of frost into bright, filtered light with high humidity; Fortuna was bred specifically to simplify crossandra care and tolerates average home and patio conditions better than older seed-grown types.

directions: Fortuna is a compact, densely branching crossandra selection bred to be more forgiving of average indoor and patio conditions than older seed strains, packing its bright orange, fan-shaped florets into a tight, cone-like spike above glossy dark-green leaves. It flowers over an unusually long season, from spring well into fall outdoors and nearly year-round as a warm, bright indoor plant. Keep the growing medium evenly moist but never soggy, since crossandra drops flower buds quickly if it dries out, and use lime-free or rain water where tap water is hard. Provide bright, indirect light rather than harsh direct sun, and keep it away from cold drafts and heating vents, since it is sensitive to both chill and dry air.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after all danger of frost into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in bright shade to filtered morning sun; Sundance holds a neat, rounded shape without pinching, making it a reliable choice for mixed containers and border edges.

directions: Sundance is a compact, uniformly rounded crossandra selection that stays under about 16 inches without pinching, carrying vivid orange, fan-shaped flowers in tight spikes above glossy foliage from spring into fall. Its tidy, even habit makes it especially useful for mixed container plantings and the front of shaded borders, where taller, looser crossandra types can flop or need staking. Keep soil consistently moist and fertilize lightly on a monthly schedule during active growth to sustain its long bloom period. In the Gulf South it performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, and it should be brought indoors or given heavy mulch protection well before the first frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after all danger of frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida Flame carries a more upright, spreading habit than the dwarf pot-culture crossandra selections and fills out a bed more quickly.

directions: Florida Flame is an upright-to-spreading crossandra selection distinguished from the softer salmon tones of Orange Marmalade and the dwarf habit of Mona Wallhed by its deeper reddish-orange flower spikes carried on a taller, more open frame. It blooms continuously from spring through frost outdoors in frost-free zones, or year-round where grown as a warm greenhouse or container specimen. Because of its larger stature it fills a bed faster than the compact pot-culture cultivars and works well as a mid-border accent in shaded tropical plantings. Provide consistently moist, fertile soil and protection from harsh midday sun, and cut plants back by about a third in late winter where they persist as short-lived perennials to keep growth dense and floriferous.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions
